 The last 24 hours have been pretty stellar across the neighborhood after Saturday kicked off rather wet and gloomy. Since then, conditions have improved noticeably! Although, I'm sure fast moving showers on Doppler 3x may not have been on Monday's bingo card for a lot of you. We've had a leftover pulse of energy wandering across the state northeast to southwest. This is something we call a "secondary cold push" often found behind a strong initial wave of cooler drier air. This is especially the case as we start building an area of low pressure off the Mid-Atlantic coast. That same spin is actually what's tagged by the National Hurricane Center for possible subtropical development. 
 All in all, today marks the transition towards even better weather as we move throughout the week. Believe it or not, despite being marked in orange on the NHC's page, the low trying to further organize is actually helping our local forecast rather than hurting whatsoever. Tomorrow we'll dry the atmosphere out further, removing the chance of any isolated or scattered showers like we've observed today.
 That also means skies should remain mostly clear for the SpaceX launch scheduled first thing tomorrow morning. The winds will stay elevated because of such a pressure difference to our north into south Florida. That's going to help filter out the nocturnal showers tonight and create even better conditions tomorrow and ahead. 
 A small craft advisory is in effect until 3am tonight. National Weather Service should be allowed to let this advisory go. But, given we're keeping winds in your forecast, you'll still see some chop out there on the water if you do get on the boat. Otherwise, your Weather Authority isn't tracking any other impediments to your day to day. 
 The tropics are quiet outside of our tagged non-tropical system. If it takes its time, and stews over the warm Gulf stream its currently positioned over, it may develop some thunderstorms near its center. That's why despite the non-tropical origin, it has a modest shot at taking on a more subtropical look. We do want this to meander further, and gain a little more strength, to keep our weather pleasant down here! As always, stick with your Weather Authority for everything you need to know about this fall stretch of weather, and what goes on off the east coast with our low pressure center.
